Section 1: Library Workshop Booking

Librarian: Good morning, City Library. How can I help you?
Reader: Hi, I'd like to book a place on the digital skills workshop next week. Is it still available?
Librarian: Let me check the schedule for you. We have two sessions: Tuesday at 10 a.m. and Thursday at 2 p.m. Which one would you prefer?
Reader: I think Thursday would be better for me. But wait, is the Thursday session in the morning or afternoon?
Librarian: It's at 2 p.m., in the afternoon. The Tuesday one is at 10 a.m.
Reader: OK, Thursday at 2 p.m. is fine. How long does it last?
Librarian: Each session lasts two hours, so it finishes at 4 p.m.
Reader: Good. And how much does it cost?
Librarian: It's free for library members. Are you a member?
Reader: Yes, I joined last month. My membership number is 4472.
Librarian: Great. Can I take your name and phone number, please?
Reader: Sure. My name is Sarah Chen. My phone number is 0789 123 456.
Librarian: Sorry, could you repeat the phone number?
Reader: Yes, it's 0789 123 456.
Librarian: Thank you. Now, do you have any experience with computers?
Reader: A little. I can use email and search the internet, but I'm not very confident with spreadsheets.
Librarian: That's fine. The workshop covers basic spreadsheet skills. You'll need to bring your own laptop if you have one. Do you have a laptop?
Reader: Yes, I do. Should I bring anything else?
Librarian: Just a notebook and pen if you want to take notes. We provide the software.
Reader: OK. Is there a maximum number of people in the class?
Librarian: Yes, the maximum is 12 people. There are still 3 places left for Thursday.
Reader: That's good. So I'd like to book one place for Thursday.
Librarian: Certainly. I've booked you in. You'll receive a confirmation email. What's your email address?
Reader: It's sarah.chen@email.com.
Librarian: Let me repeat that: sarah.chen@email.com. Is that correct?
Reader: Yes, that's right.
Librarian: One more thing: the workshop is in the computer room on the second floor, not the main hall. The main hall is being painted.
Reader: Thanks for telling me. I'll go to the second floor.
Librarian: Perfect. See you on Thursday at 2 p.m.
Reader: Thank you. Goodbye.

Section 2: Library Orientation: Reading Under Time Pressure

Hello everyone, and welcome to the Westbridge Community Library. My name is Sarah, and I'm the head librarian here. Today I'll give you some practical information about using our library, especially for those of you who are preparing for exams or doing research under time pressure. This orientation is designed to help you make the most of our resources.

First, let me explain our opening hours. We are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Saturdays. We are closed on Sundays and public holidays. Please note that the library is busiest between 4 and 6 p.m. on weekdays, so if you prefer a quiet space, come earlier in the day.

Now, about borrowing books. You can borrow up to 10 items at a time. Books can be kept for three weeks, and you can renew them twice, as long as no one else has reserved them. DVDs, however, can only be borrowed for one week. You cannot renew DVDs. If you return items late, you will be charged a fine of 50 cents per day per item. The maximum fine for any single item is 10 dollars.

We have a special collection for exam preparation. These books are located on the second floor, near the study area. They are marked with a red sticker. You can borrow them for two weeks only, and they cannot be renewed. This is because they are in high demand. If you need a book that is already borrowed, you can place a reservation online or at the front desk. We will send you an email when it becomes available.

Our study areas are on the first and second floors. The first floor is for group study, and you can talk there, but please keep your voice down. The second floor is a silent zone, so no talking is allowed. There are also individual study carrels on the third floor, which you can book for up to two hours at a time. To book a carrel, use the self-service machine near the stairs.

We also offer free Wi-Fi. The network name is 'Westbridge Library', and the password is 'readmore2024'. You can connect for up to three hours per day. After that, you need to log in again.

Finally, I'd like to mention our workshops. Every Wednesday at 6 p.m., we run a workshop on speed reading and exam strategies. These are free for library members, but you need to sign up in advance because places are limited to 15 people. You can sign up at the front desk or on our website.

That's all for now. If you have any questions, please ask at the front desk. Thank you for listening.

Section 3: Time-Limited Reading: True/False/Not Given and Evidence Scope

Tutor: Today we're discussing evidence in time-limited reading tests. Each mini-text is independent, so don't carry facts from one example into another. Maria, what slows you down?
Maria: I search for identical words. If the statement uses different wording, I keep looking even when the meaning seems clear.
Tutor: The first rule is: look for the meaning, not identical words. A paraphrase can agree with a text without repeating its wording. False means the text contradicts the statement.
John: So if a library is described as closed on Sundays, a statement saying it's open then is False?
Tutor: Yes. Now suppose another mini-text says, 'The library is open on weekdays only.' What about Sunday opening?
John: 'Weekdays only' excludes Sunday, so that statement is False too.
Maria: What if a text says some students prefer online learning? Does that make a statement about all students False?
Tutor: Not automatically. Quantifiers matter. From 'some' alone, 'all' is Not Given, not automatically False. Some establishes a preference among at least part of the group; it doesn't establish whether everyone shares it. An explicit exception would contradict 'all'.
Maria: Such as one student who prefers classroom study instead?
Tutor: Exactly. Distinguish a claim that hasn't been proved from one that has been disproved.
John: And if a separate text says the library has many books, can I accept a claim that it has more than ten thousand?
Tutor: No. The text doesn't give a specific number of books. 'Many' doesn't establish that threshold, but it doesn't contradict it either.
Maria: What about 'The library was open on Sundays last year'? Does that establish Sunday opening now?
Tutor: No. Past tense alone does not establish a present situation. Pay attention to time words such as 'last year', 'now' and 'in the past'. A schedule may continue or change; neither outcome has been stated here.
John: Comparisons need the same care. If the new library is larger than the old one, reversing the comparison changes the claim.
Tutor: Right. Comparisons can be reversed to create false statements. Now here's one complete practice text: 'The city library opens at nine on weekdays. It closes at eight on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, but at six on Tuesdays and Thursdays. It is closed on weekends.'
Maria: Then Tuesday closing is six, not eight.
John: And a statement about Saturday opening would be False, because Saturday is part of the weekend.
Tutor: Finally, take a separate text saying only that a library does not lend DVDs. That doesn't tell us whether it lends CDs. Check what the negation applies to; don't extend it to an unmentioned category.
Maria: So we need evidence for either agreement or contradiction?
Tutor: Yes. Let's summarise: check meaning, scope, quantities, comparisons and time. When the required relationship is missing, don't fill the gap with outside knowledge.

Section 4: The Economics of Time-Limited Reading: Judgement and Evidence Scope

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a skill that is becoming increasingly important in academic and professional settings: time-limited reading. Specifically, I will focus on two related aspects: making true/false/not given judgements and understanding the scope of evidence. These are crucial for anyone who needs to read quickly and accurately under pressure.

Let me start with a common misconception. Many people believe that speed reading is simply about moving your eyes faster across the page. However, research in cognitive psychology suggests that comprehension depends more on how you process information than on raw speed. In fact, trying to read too quickly can actually reduce your understanding, because you may miss key details or misinterpret the author's meaning.

So, what is the scope of evidence? When you answer a true/false/not given question, you must base your answer strictly on the information provided in the passage. You should not use your own knowledge or make assumptions beyond what is written. For example, if a passage says 'Some students find time-limited reading challenging,' you cannot conclude that 'All students find it challenging.' The word 'some' limits the scope. Similarly, if the passage mentions 'a 2019 study,' you cannot assume the findings apply to other years unless stated.

Now, let's consider the role of grammar in interpreting meaning. Negation, comparison, quantifiers, and tense all affect the scope of evidence. Take negation: if a sentence says 'The researcher did not find a significant difference,' it means no difference was found, not that a difference exists. Comparison: 'Reading speed increased more than comprehension' tells you that both improved, but speed improved to a greater extent. Quantifiers: words like 'all,' 'most,' 'some,' and 'few' indicate different ranges. For instance, 'Most participants completed the task' does not mean 'All participants completed it.' Tense: 'The study showed' (past) versus 'The study shows' (present) can indicate whether findings are considered established or limited to that specific study.

Let me give you an example from a reading test. Suppose the passage states: 'In the 2020 experiment, participants who read under time pressure scored lower on comprehension tests than those who read without time limits.' A question might ask: 'Participants in the 2020 experiment who read under time pressure scored higher than those who did not.' The answer is False, because the passage explicitly says 'lower,' not 'higher.' Another question: 'The 2020 experiment included participants of all ages.' The passage does not mention ages, so the answer is Not Given. You must not infer that all ages were included; the information is simply absent.

A key strategy is to locate the relevant part of the passage and check the exact wording. Do not rely on memory or general impressions. Also, pay attention to distractors: sometimes a question uses words from the passage but changes the relationship, such as reversing cause and effect or swapping comparison direction.

In summary, time-limited reading requires careful attention to evidence scope. Always ask: What exactly does the text say? Does it use limiting words like 'some' or 'most'? Is the tense significant? By mastering these, you can improve both speed and accuracy. Thank you.

grammar.title: 否定、比较、数量范围和时态；限定词的含义
grammar.explanation: 英语中否定词（not, no, never）改变句子意思；比较级（better, more）用于比较；数量限定词（some, any, many, much, a few, a little）表示数量范围；时态（现在完成时、一般过去时等）表示时间关系。限定词如 'the' 表示特指，'a/an' 表示泛指。
